short: HITRUST CSF is a certifiable security framework from HITRUST, a private standards body. It underlies three certifications, e1, i1 and r2, and since late 2024 an AI Security Certification for deployed AI systems. It is not a law and HIPAA does not require it.
title: HITRUST CSF
subtitle: The HITRUST Framework, its e1, i1 and r2 certifications, and its AI security certification
body_html:
HITRUST CSF, which HITRUST now also calls the HITRUST Framework, is a certifiable set of security controls published by HITRUST, a private standards and assurance body. It is the control set behind three certifications of rising depth, called e1, i1 and r2. Since late 2024 it also carries an AI Security Certification for organizations that deploy AI systems. It is not a law, and HIPAA does not require it. Organizations use it because a HITRUST certificate is widely accepted as evidence in vendor risk reviews, above all in healthcare.

What is HITRUST CSF?

HITRUST describes the framework as the foundational control set for all of its assessments, so that results are consistent and comparable from one organization to the next. It draws requirements from many standards and regulations into one set, which is why a single assessment can be reported against several of them. HITRUST also describes the framework as threat adaptive: it says it analyzes threat intelligence and breach data and updates control requirements in response, on a quarterly cycle. By its own account the framework harmonizes more than 70 authoritative sources, including NIST, ISO and PCI.

An assessment is carried out by a HITRUST Authorized External Assessor, of which HITRUST says there are more than 100 firms, and then reviewed centrally by HITRUST, which issues the report or the certification. That second review is the difference from a self attestation, and it is what buyers are relying on when they accept the certificate.

What is the difference between e1, i1 and r2?

All three are built on the same framework, so work done for a smaller assessment carries into a larger one. HITRUST calls the set traversable for that reason.

AssessmentWhat HITRUST says it is forSize
e1Essential cybersecurity hygiene, the entry point44 requirement statements
i1A moderate level of assurance covering leading practices and a broader range of active threats than e1, with no tailoring of controls182 requirement statements in year one, about 60 in year two with rapid recertification
r2The highest assurance, tailored to the organization's risk factors and scored with a control maturity modelVaries with scope. Certification lasts two years.

An organization can also inherit controls from a cloud provider that is itself HITRUST certified, which reduces the work for anything the provider already covers.

What does HITRUST offer for AI?

Two things. The first is the AI Security Assessment and Certification, announced in a HITRUST advisory dated December 6, 2024. As of version 11.4.0 of the framework it consists of up to 44 requirement statements aimed at the security of deployed AI systems. HITRUST says the controls align with the AI security elements of ISO, NIST and OWASP publications. At launch the AI assessment had to be added to an e1, i1 or r2 assessment, and HITRUST now says the certification is also available on its own.

The controls are not one fixed list. HITRUST says they are selected for the AI deployment scenario, according to inherent risk and the kind of model involved, which is why the count is given as up to 44. It built them by reviewing nearly two dozen sources on AI security threats, ISO, NIST and OWASP among them, against its own framework. It is aimed at AI application providers and AI platform providers, meaning firms that sell AI systems to other organizations or build AI into their own products. As with the core assessments, AI controls can be inherited from a cloud provider whose systems are already certified, and HITRUST says the major cloud providers took part in developing it.

The second is the AI Risk Management Assessment, which HITRUST describes as 51 AI risk management controls harmonized with ISO 23894 and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. It reports results in ISO and NIST terms. It is an assessment for insight, not the same thing as the security certification.

For a buyer the practical point is narrow. A vendor's ordinary HITRUST certificate says nothing about its AI systems. Ask whether the AI Security Certification is included and which system it covers.

When did AI enter the HITRUST CSF, and what does it ask for?

In stages. Schellman, an audit firm that is a HITRUST assessor, reported in November 2023 that version 11.2.0 of the framework added AI risk management content, mapped to the NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0, ISO/IEC 23894 and ISO 31000. An organization pursuing an r2 certification could select AI risk management as a factor when scoping the assessment. The separate AI Security Assessment followed in December 2024, and by version 11.4.0 it stood at up to 44 requirement statements.

Schellman's account of version 11.2.0 is the clearest public description of what the AI factor asks an organization to show. Requirement details change between versions, so treat this as the shape of the evidence and confirm the current text with HITRUST or your assessor.

Area of the frameworkWhat the AI factor added, per Schellman
Information protection programDocumented internal and external context for AI use, including effects on staff, transparency of the systems, legal and contractual duties, and wider societal impact. A documented AI risk process covering criteria, identification and analysis.
Risk managementA stated commitment to AI risk management shared with stakeholders. Human behavior and culture considered in AI risk assessment. Societal and individual impact analyses of AI systems at least once a year. Documented consideration of the potential for harm to people, to human rights and to the environment.
Vulnerability managementAI data, models and systems included in a documented inventory.
Business continuityA business impact analysis of AI systems at least once a year.

Two things are worth noticing. Most of what is asked for is documentation and recurring analysis, not new technology. And the first item anyone will ask for is the inventory, because every other requirement depends on knowing which AI systems exist.

Is HITRUST the same as HIPAA compliance?

No. HIPAA is federal law, enforced by the Office for Civil Rights at the Department of Health and Human Services. HITRUST is a private framework. No regulator has said that holding a HITRUST certificate makes an organization HIPAA compliant.

What HITRUST does offer is a mapping. Its Insights Reports restate assessment results in the language of a specific standard, HIPAA among them, so that one assessment can answer several questionnaires. See HIPAA and AI and HHS OCR enforcement for the law itself.

How does HITRUST compare with SOC 2 and ISO 27001?

They answer different questions. A SOC 2 report is an auditor's opinion on controls the organization chose, measured against the AICPA trust services criteria. ISO 27001 certifies a management system. HITRUST prescribes the controls themselves and scores the organization against them, which makes two HITRUST results easier to compare than two SOC 2 reports.

Many data center and cloud operators hold all three. On this site you will see HITRUST listed beside SOC 2, ISO 27001 and PCI DSS on data center facility pages, because healthcare tenants ask for it.

Why do insurers and vendor risk teams care?

HITRUST names the audiences it built the AI certification for, and two of them matter to readers of this site. Third party risk management programs can use it to check that a vendor employing AI has secured it. HITRUST also names the cyber insurance industry, saying insurers can use the certification as a repeatable instrument for understanding the residual AI risk they are underwriting. That is HITRUST describing its own product, not an insurer confirming that it prices on it. For how carriers are actually treating AI risk, see AI Insurance.

What should you make of the breach free claim?

HITRUST states that 99.62 percent of HITRUST certified environments reported no breaches in 2025. That is the organization's own figure about its own program, and it rests on what certified organizations reported. It is worth knowing, and it should be read as a vendor statistic and not as an independent finding.

This page is reference material, not legal or audit advice. Requirement counts change with each framework version, so confirm them against HITRUST before you scope an assessment.
